hints: Notice that area 1 lies above the time axis where velocity is positive, while area 2 lies below the time axis where velocity is negative.
Recall that displacement is the signed area under a velocity-time graph, so motion back toward the start subtracts from forward motion.
Compare what happens if you add the two area magnitudes versus subtracting the backward part to get net change in position.
walkthrough: Look at the axes: velocity is plotted against time, so the area between the curve and the time axis represents change in position.
State the rule: $\text{displacement} = \text{area under velocity-time graph}$, with area above the axis counted positive and area below the axis counted negative.
Area 1 is above the axis with $v > 0$, so it contributes $+\text{area 1}$ to displacement for motion in the forward direction.
Area 2 is below the axis with $v < 0$, so its velocity is negative and it contributes $-\text{area 2}$ to displacement for motion in the opposite direction.
Add the signed contributions: $\text{total displacement} = (+\text{area 1}) + (-\text{area 2}) = \text{area 1} - \text{area 2}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Area 1 is positive displacement and area 2 is negative displacement, so total displacement is $\text{area 1} - \text{area 2}$.

B.explanation: Dividing by 2 has no meaning here; the whole area under a velocity-time graph already equals displacement.

C.explanation: Adding the magnitudes gives total distance travelled, not total displacement which keeps the sign of velocity.

D.explanation: This reverses the signs and would give a negative value when the forward motion in area 1 is larger.
